evidence: Plaut. Most. 627: nōn ego istuc cūrō quī sit quid sit unde sit
Cic. N. D. 2.167: magna dī cūrant, parva neglegunt
terms.comment: With an accusative or a question; with a negative it is “I don’t care”: nōn cūrō, nihil cūrō.

evidence: Caes. BG 1.33 (Lewis & Short): sibi eam rem cūrae futūram
terms.comment: With a dative of the person: mihi cūrae est, I care about it, I’ll see to it.

evidence: Cic. Fam. 16.4.3: nihil labōrō, nisi ut salvus sīs
terms.comment: With dē and the ablative, or ut and the subjunctive; nōn labōrō, it doesn’t trouble me (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: I don’t care for, I can do without
terms.comment: With an accusative; Lewis & Short: “to care nothing about it”. Nōn moror is also “I don’t mind” (see mind, object).

terms.gloss: I don't give a hoot about
terms.grammar: floccī, genitive of value (“at a tuft of wool”), with facere
terms.register: vōx sermōnis cotīdiānī: Plaut.; Cic. in epistulīs
evidence: Plaut. Rud. 3.5.3: ego, quae tū loquere, floccī nōn faciō (Lewis & Short), s.v. floccus
Cic. Att. 13.50.3: nec tamen floccī faciō (Lewis & Short)
Traupman p. 100: eum floccī nōn faciō

phrases.latin: Nōn ego istuc cūrō quī sit quid sit unde sit
phrases.english: I don’t care who he is, what he is or where he comes from.

phrases.latin: nūllā in rē jam tē festīnāre volō; nihil labōrō, nisi ut salvus sīs
phrases.english: I don’t want you to hurry over anything now; all I care about is that you get well.
The gods care about great things and neglect the small ones.
